Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> Features | National | Opinion Open Letter To the Government: Who’s protecting young Ghanaians travelling to Russia? Are they safe? Source : Ebenezer Afanyi Dadzie 16 November 2026 8:29pm President Mahama recently met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Russia during the Russia-African Summit. ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
Dear President John Dramani Mahama and Honourable Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa, Minister for Foreign Affairs,
I write as a concerned Ghanaian journalist, increasingly worried about reports of young Ghanaians being lured into the Russia-Ukraine war, with some losing their lives, others ending up as prisoners of war and several more remaining missing.
My concern is not about Ghana's diplomatic relations with Russia or an attempt to discourage legitimate educational and employment opportunities abroad, in general. It is about the responsibility of government to protect Ghanaian citizens, particularly young people who may be vulnerable to deception and exploitation.
My question is simple but urgent: What specific safety and security alerts are being given to young Ghanaians travelling to Russia, particularly students and beneficiaries of scholarship programmes, to ensure they do not become victims of recruitment networks allegedly luring foreigners into the war?
This question has become even more pertinent following the disturbing revelations about Ghanaians who have died or gone missing in the conflict and the recent departure of scholarship beneficiaries to Russia.
This is no longer speculation. Ghana's own Foreign Affairs Minister, Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa, has repeatedly confirmed the scale of the problem following engagements with Ukrainian authorities.
In February 2026, following his visit to Ukraine, the Minister disclosed that at least 55 Ghanaians had been killed while fighting in the Russia-Ukraine war, with two others being held as prisoners of war.
He also revealed that approximately 272 Ghanaians had been lured into the conflict since 2022 through transnational recruitment networks. Across Africa, an estimated 1,780 people from 36 countries were believed to have been recruited to fight for Russia.
Some of the affected Ghanaians were reportedly attracted by opportunities advertised as civilian employment, including construction, hospitality, logistics and security jobs, only to find themselves involved in the war.
The situation became even more troubling in August 2026 when Mr Ablakwa disclosed that the number of Ghanaians killed had risen to 62, with another 15 missing.
Read Also: 62 Ghanaians killed, 15 missing in Russia-Ukraine war – Ablakwa
Speaking during his visit to Russia, the Minister reiterated Ghana's concerns and efforts to engage Russian authorities to address the situation.
His position was particularly emphatic: "This is not our war, and it should not be claiming Ghanaian lives."
These are not merely statistics. They represent families whose sons, brothers, husbands and relatives may never return home. They represent young people who may have travelled in search of better economic opportunities but ended up fighting in a war in which Ghana has no stake.
The government must therefore move beyond expressing concern and prioritise preventive measures.
John Dumelo's scholarship initiative: An opportunity, but are the necessary precautions being taken?
My immediate concern was heightened by the recent announcement by the Member of Parliament for Ayawaso West Wuogon and Deputy Minister for Food and Agriculture, John Dumelo, that the first batch of beneficiaries under his scholarship initiative had departed Ghana for Russia to pursue further studies.
The initiative is expected to support more than 40 students by the end of 2027.
The effort could be viewed as commendable. At a time when many Ghanaian families struggle to finance tertiary education, providing young people with opportunities to study abroad deserves recognition.
However, while I welcomed the announcement, I could not help but ask some uncomfortable questions.
What happens when these young people arrive in Russia? Who takes responsibility for their safety beyond providing scholarships and admission arrangements?
Have they received adequate security orientation about the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war and reports of foreign nationals being lured into the Russian military?
Have they been warned about individuals or organisations that may approach them with attractive financial offers, employment opportunities or promises of a better life in exchange for signing military contracts?
Do they know that some Ghanaians reportedly travelled to Russia for civilian employment but eventually ended up on the battlefield?
Have their sponsors established reliable channels through which their welfare can be monitored throughout their stay?
And have their parents and guardians been informed about the potential risks and provided with emergency contacts should anything go wrong?
I raise these questions without suggesting that Mr Dumelo's scholarship initiative is connected in any way to the reported recruitment activities. There is no basis for such an allegation.
My concern is that a good educational opportunity can become a vulnerable entry point for exploitation if beneficiaries are not adequately prepared and protected.
The fact that these young people are travelling primarily to study does not automatically make them immune to approaches by individuals seeking to exploit their financial circumstances, ambitions or unfamiliarity with the country.
I would therefore expect that every Ghanaian public official, institution or individual facilitating educational opportunities in Russia works closely with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ghana's diplomatic mission to ensure that beneficiaries receive proper security briefings before departure.
The question is whether we are doing enough to ensure they return safely after completing their studies.
Ghana-Russia labour recruitment agreement: Are adequate safeguards in place?
My concerns are further heightened by another development reported by Citi Newsroom on October 29, 2026.
According to the report, Ghana signed an agreement with Russia to facilitate the recruitment of Ghanaian workers for industrial and manufacturing jobs.
The agreement was signed by Labour Minister Emmanuel Agyekum and the director of Russia's Alabuga Special Economic Zone, an industrial hub comprising 48 companies with a reported requirement for more than 75,000 workers. Alabuga is a name known to many. Stories have been published about young women being tricked into going to Alabuga to work in drone factories used by Russia to attack Ukraine.
Under the arrangement, Ghana's Labour Ministry is expected to coordinate recruitment, verify job offers and provide pre-departure orientation to safeguard the interests of Ghanaian workers.
While creating legitimate employment opportunities for young Ghanaians is commendable, the timing of this agreement raises important questions that the government must address.
Considering the disturbing reports of Ghanaians being lured to Russia with promises of lucrative civilian employment before allegedly ending up on the battlefield, what additional safeguards have been incorporated into this agreement to prevent a recurrence?
What specific companies will employ the Ghanaian workers, what jobs will they perform, and who will independently verify their employment contracts and working conditions?
Will the government ensure that every prospective worker understands the nature of the job, the terms of engagement, their rights and the procedures for leaving employment should the circumstances differ from what was promised?
More importantly, what guarantees exist that these workers will not be approached, pressured or deceived into signing military contracts after arriving in Russia?
The Labour Minister's assurance that the Ministry will verify job offers and provide pre-departure orientation is important. But given what Ghana has already experienced, I believe the government must go further by establishing independent monitoring, accessible complaint mechanisms and clear protections against any attempt to recruit these workers into military service.
We cannot be facilitating the movement of Ghanaian workers to Russia through official government arrangements without first demonstrating that we have put adequate safeguards in place to protect them.
The opportunity to work abroad should never become a pathway to a foreign battlefield.
Ghana has received warnings from Ukrainian authorities about the dangers facing its citizens in Russia.
During his February 2026 visit to Kyiv, Mr Ablakwa held discussions with his Ukrainian counterpart, Andrii Sybiha, who raised concerns about the recruitment of African nationals into the Russian military.
The Ukrainian Foreign Minister warned that Africans, including Ghanaians, were being drawn into the conflict through deceptive recruitment arrangements.
More recently, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, addressing the 81st United Nations General Assembly in September 2026, identified Ghana among 47 countries whose citizens, he said, were being used in Russia's war against Ukraine.
Read Also: ‘Do not let Russia pay for its madness with lives of your people’ – Zelensky to Ghana, 46 other countries
He urged the affected countries to protect their nationals and prevent them from ending up on the battlefield, highlighting the use of deception and other tactics to recruit foreign nationals.
What more warning does our government need to appreciate the urgency of this situation?
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has previously issued travel advisories cautioning Ghanaians against travelling to conflict areas and warning them about middlemen and agents who promise employment and other opportunities in countries experiencing armed conflict.
We now have official figures indicating that dozens of Ghanaians have died, others are missing, and some have been captured as prisoners of war.
The question is whether the Ministry has moved beyond general travel advisories to a targeted and sustained public education campaign addressing the dangers facing Ghanaians travelling to Russia.
How many prospective students are aware of the reported recruitment tactics?
How many travel agencies, universities and educational facilitators have been engaged?
It is not enough for the Ministry to issue statements on its website or social media platforms and assume that everyone who needs the information has received it.
A warning is only useful when it reaches the people it is intended to protect.
It is also important to acknowledge that Russia has rejected allegations of deliberately recruiting African nationals unlawfully into its military. Russian Ambassador to Ghana, Andrei Ordash, has maintained that foreign nationals can voluntarily enlist through contractual arrangements under Russian law.
However, the concern is not simply that a Ghanaian may voluntarily choose to join a foreign military. It is that people travelling in search of legitimate civilian employment or educational opportunities could allegedly be deceived, coerced or manipulated into participating in a war.
Ghana cannot leave the protection of its citizens entirely to assurances from foreign governments.
At the recent Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, President John Dramani Mahama raised Ghana's concerns about recruiting its citizens into the Russia-Ukraine war during bilateral discussions with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
According to the Ghanaian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, President Putin gave an assurance that Ghanaians would no longer be permitted to participate in the war.
The commitment, as communicated by the Ghanaian government, is expected to address both irregular recruitment arrangements and voluntary enlistment.
The development is welcome, and President Mahama deserves commendation for raising an issue that has caused so much pain to Ghanaian families.
However, is President Putin's assurance sufficient reason for Ghana to relax its vigilance and allow its citizens, particularly young people, to continue travelling to Russia without comprehensive security education and precautionary measures?
A diplomatic assurance, however significant, must be followed by practical measures, monitoring and accountability. The government must also ensure that recruitment networks allegedly operating to lure unsuspecting Africans are identified and dismantled.
What happens to the 15 Ghanaians reported missing? What about those already in captivity or serving in the Russian military? How will Ghana verify that the commitment announced after the summit is being implemented?
Mr President and Honourable Minister, I believe the time has come for Ghana to introduce a more deliberate security education programme for all Ghanaians travelling to Russia.
These measures are not intended to discourage legitimate educational or economic relations with Russia. They are intended to ensure that such relations do not expose Ghanaian citizens to preventable dangers.
Our young people deserve opportunities, but above all, they deserve protection
Ghana has every right to pursue diplomatic, economic and educational partnerships with Russia. There is nothing inherently wrong with Ghanaian students travelling there to acquire knowledge, build careers and contribute to national development.
But we must not let the excitement around international opportunities overshadow the realities confronting some of our citizens.
When 62 Ghanaians have reportedly died, and 15 others are missing in a foreign war, we cannot afford to treat the matter as an ordinary diplomatic disagreement.
When the Ukrainian President has specifically mentioned Ghana among countries whose citizens are allegedly being lured into the conflict, our response must go beyond statements of concern.
And when our own Foreign Affairs Minister acknowledges that criminal networks are exploiting young Ghanaians through deceptive employment arrangements, the government must ensure that prospective travellers understand those dangers before leaving the country.
I am particularly worried that, in our enthusiasm to promote international educational opportunities, we may be overlooking the need to educate young people about the security implications of travelling to a country involved in an active war.
A scholarship should be an opportunity to acquire an education, not an avenue through which a young person becomes vulnerable to exploitation. A job offer should provide an opportunity to earn a living, not become a deceptive pathway to the battlefield.
Mr President and Honourable Minister, Ghanaians should not have to choose between pursuing opportunities abroad and remaining safe. The government must find a way to guarantee both.
My question, therefore, remains: Following the deaths, disappearances and imprisonment of several Ghanaians in the Russia-Ukraine war, what specific safety and security alerts are being given to young Ghanaians travelling to Russia today, and what concrete measures are in place to ensure they are not lured into this war?
President Putin may have given his assurance, but can Ghana afford to simply look on and watch its young people travel to Russia without first ensuring that they understand the risks and know how to protect themselves?
We have already lost too many lives. We should not wait for another Ghanaian family to receive devastating news before taking preventive action.
The government's responsibility is not only to negotiate the safe return of citizens who have fallen victim to dangerous circumstances. It is also to prevent more citizens from becoming victims in the first place.
Our young people deserve opportunities. But above all, they deserve to live long enough to benefit from them.
Yours in the interest of Ghana and the protection of its citizens,
